title: A small design change made two hotel walkways collapse
body: On 17 July 1981, two suspended walkways crashed into a crowded hotel atrium in Kansas City, killing 114 people. The original design hung both walkways from shared long rods. During construction this was changed so the lower walkway hung from the upper one. The change, approved without proper checking, doubled the load on the upper walkway’s connections, which were already weaker than the building code required.

slides.heading: The original design
slides.text: Single long rods ran from the ceiling through both walkways. Each walkway rested on nuts on those rods, so each connection held up only its own walkway.

slides.heading: The change
slides.text: To make construction easier, each rod was split in two: one set hung the upper walkway from the ceiling, and a second set hung the lower walkway from the upper one.

slides.heading: Why it failed
slides.text: The upper connections now carried both walkways and the crowd on them. During a tea dance, the rods and nuts pulled through the beams of the upper walkway.

slides.heading: The aftermath
slides.text: The engineers of record lost their licences in Missouri, and the case is now taught worldwide as a lesson in checking design changes.
